doc.title: Victor Rendon interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, November 15, 2019 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Respect for tradition, women and the sacred drums
summary: Using the rhythms in novelty settings, restrictions on women, and a student asking whether he must join the religion.

story.theme_name: Church, faith and religion in a musician's life
story.community_name: Church, faith and jazz: the sacred and the secular

blocks.x: Okay. You think of the, like the Miami Sound Machine or some novelty hits like the Macarena —

Yeah it’s okay. As long as it’s not disrespecting the culture or the tradition or the drums or the rhythms themselves, in my opinion you can do just about anything. Oh yes, women are not supposed to touch the sacred drums also, there’s a whole thing about that. But as they get older now I hear it has to do something with menopause and you know, the period. Because blood is not good when you’re around the deities. So supposedly they feed on that. So I shouldn’t be talking too much about that.

Well it’s part of the culture. And I was sort of thinking after I was learning about this stuff yesterday, that all religions have — they have icons. You know the Catholic religion has its icon, it has symbols, it has physical movements, and the religion that you’re talking about has its drums.

Exactly. But as long as you play them like — a student of mine asked me, because he’s learning batá , and he comes every Sunday to me where we have the class. He’s learning very quickly. He says, “Do I have to be part of the religion? You know. No you don’t. You can play as much as you want. Later on when you’ve reached that stage, you have to make a decision how far you want to take it as far as that spiritual side of it is involved. But it doesn’t have to be. You can play the drums as much as you want. A woman can learn as much as she wants. And there’s no research on that.
